title: MIT Professor Uses AI to Make Power-Hungry Data Centers More Efficient
summary:
Huge buildings filled with computers, called data centers, use so much electricity that they can strain power grids and increase demand for energy from fossil fuels. Christina Delimitrou, a newly tenured associate professor at MIT, is trying to shrink that environmental cost by changing how servers and networks inside data centers work.

Her group uses machine learning to make large cloud systems more efficient, secure, and reliable. They redesign older cloud software, manage shared hardware more carefully, and design leaner servers so operators can get more computing done with the machines they already have.

"If data centers are not utilized to the best of their capabilities, then they will burn much more power than they need to meet growing user demand," Delimitrou said. She noted that software often includes extra "bloating," and removing it without hurting performance could mean fewer new data centers need to be built.

Her team also uses AI to help programmers find and fix problems in cloud apps such as music streaming or video calls, which can cut downtime that wastes computing power. Better resource management, she said, can give phone users more predictable performance.

Earlier research with mentor Christos Kozyrakis found many large systems ran at only about 15 percent capacity even when demand was high. Machine learning can automate resource choices that are hard for people to manage at the scale of tens of thousands of machines.

Delimitrou grew up in northern Greece, studied computer engineering in Athens, earned a Ph.D. at Stanford, taught at Cornell, and now works in MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and CSAIL. Her work shows how smarter software—not only more buildings—can answer growing demand for cloud computing.
why_it_matters: Cloud apps kids use every day run in data centers. Smarter software can mean less wasted electricity and a smaller environmental footprint.
